title: A good deal
stem:
You are an F2 doctor on a cardiology ward. Mr Doyle, 58, who owns a car dealership, is being discharged after a heart attack.

He thanks you, and offers you £3,000 off any car at his garage.
instruction: Rank in order the following actions in response to this situation (1 = Most appropriate; 5 = Least appropriate).

options.text: Accept, as he has been discharged.
options.detailed: He may need further care, and accepting a large benefit could still affect, or be seen to affect, your judgement.

options.text: Accept, and ask him to keep it between you.
options.detailed: Asking for secrecy shows you know it is wrong. It is the least appropriate option.

options.text: Thank him warmly, and politely decline the discount.
options.brief: A large personal benefit isn't appropriate.
options.detailed: A discount this size could be seen to affect your judgement. Declining politely is the right response. It ranks first.

options.text: Check the trust's gifts and hospitality policy.
options.brief: The policy guides what can be accepted.
options.detailed: Checking the policy confirms what is acceptable. It ranks second because the right response is already clear.

options.text: Suggest he thanks the ward team with a card or a note instead.
options.detailed: This lets him show his gratitude in an appropriate way. It ranks third.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you recognise a gift that could affect, or be seen to affect, your judgement.
explanation.keyDetails: The discount is large. He is a patient. He is being discharged.
explanation.reasoning: [C] declines politely, [D] checks the policy, and [E] offers an alternative. [A] accepts a large benefit, and [B] adds secrecy.
explanation.competing: [D] and [E] are close. The key puts the policy first because it guides any decision about gifts.

references.title: Identifying and managing conflicts of interest
